% ================================================================================================ PART 1
\section{PART 1: THEORY}

A convolutional neural network (CNN) is a neural network for grid-structured data such as images
\cite{goodfellow2016}. Instead of connecting every pixel to every unit, it applies small learned filters at every
position (local connectivity and weight sharing), so the number of parameters does not depend on the image size
and a pattern is detected wherever it appears. This part summarizes only the components used by the three models
of Part~2.

\subsection{1. Convolution, pooling and fully connected layers}
A \textbf{convolutional layer} with $C_{in}$ input channels slides $C_{out}$ kernels of size $k\times k$ over the
input; output channel $o$ (a \emph{feature map}) is
\begin{equation}
  Y_o[i,j] = b_o + \sum_{c=1}^{C_{in}} \sum_{m,n} X_c[s\,i+m,\; s\,j+n]\, W_{o,c}[m,n],
  \label{eq:conv}
\end{equation}
where $s$ is the stride. The layer has $(k^2C_{in}+1)\,C_{out}$ parameters, and an input of height $H$ with padding
$p$ gives an output of height $\lfloor (H+2p-k)/s\rfloor + 1$. All our $3\times3$ convolutions use ``same''
padding, so only a stride or a pooling layer reduces the resolution. A \textbf{$1\times1$ convolution} mixes the
channels at each position and changes the number of channels cheaply \cite{lin2014}. Every convolution is followed
by the non-linearity $\mathrm{ReLU}(z)=\max(0,z)$.

\textbf{Max pooling} ($2\times2$, stride 2) keeps the maximum of each window: it halves the height and width,
enlarges the receptive field of the next layers and adds robustness to small shifts. \textbf{Global average
pooling} (GAP) averages each feature map into one number, $g_c=\frac{1}{HW}\sum_{i,j}X_c[i,j]$, turning an
$H\times W\times C$ tensor into a $C$-vector without any parameter \cite{lin2014}. Finally, \textbf{fully
connected} layers combine the features and a softmax layer outputs the class probabilities
$\hat y_k = e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j}$.

\subsection{2. CNN blocks: batch normalization and residual connections}
Modern CNNs repeat a \emph{block} rather than single layers. VGG \cite{simonyan2015} showed that two stacked
$3\times3$ convolutions cover a $5\times5$ region with fewer parameters and one more non-linearity than a single
$5\times5$ convolution. \textbf{Batch normalization} (BN) \cite{ioffe2015} normalizes every channel with the
mini-batch mean $\mu_B$ and variance $\sigma_B^2$ and applies a learned scale and shift,
\begin{equation}
  \hat x = \frac{x-\mu_B}{\sqrt{\sigma_B^2+\epsilon}}, \qquad y = \gamma\,\hat x + \beta ,
  \label{eq:bn}
\end{equation}
which stabilizes and speeds up training. \textbf{Residual learning} \cite{he2016} lets a block learn a residual
function $\mathcal F$ and adds the input back through a shortcut,
\begin{equation}
  \symbf y = \mathcal F(\symbf x) + W_s\,\symbf x ,
  \label{eq:res}
\end{equation}
where $W_s$ is the identity or, when the number of channels changes, a $1\times1$ convolution (projection). If the
best mapping is close to the identity, the block only has to push $\mathcal F$ towards zero, and the shortcut gives
the gradient a direct path to earlier layers. This is what makes very deep networks such as ResNet-50, built from 16
\emph{bottleneck} blocks ($1\times1\rightarrow3\times3\rightarrow1\times1$ convolutions), trainable.

\subsection{3. Training, regularization and transfer learning}
The networks minimize the cross-entropy. With imbalanced classes each sample is weighted by a class weight
$w_{y_i}$, so that errors on rare classes cost more \cite{he2009}:
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal L = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_{y_i}\,\log \hat y_{i,y_i}.
  \label{eq:ce}
\end{equation}
Gradients are computed by backpropagation and the weights are updated by \textbf{Adam} \cite{kingma2015},
optionally with decoupled weight decay \cite{loshchilov2019}. Over-fitting is limited by \textbf{dropout}
\cite{srivastava2014}, which randomly zeroes units during training; by \textbf{data augmentation}, which shows
label-preserving transformations of the training images; and by \textbf{early stopping} on a validation metric.
\textbf{Transfer learning} reuses a network pretrained on a large dataset such as ImageNet \cite{deng2009}, whose
early layers learn generic features \cite{yosinski2014}: a new head is first trained on the frozen backbone, then
the whole network is fine-tuned with a small learning rate.

\subsection{4. Evaluation metrics}
From the confusion matrix we count, for each class $k$, the true positives $TP_k$, false positives $FP_k$ and false
negatives $FN_k$:
\begin{equation}
  \begin{gathered}
  P_k=\frac{TP_k}{TP_k+FP_k},\qquad R_k=\frac{TP_k}{TP_k+FN_k},\qquad F1_k=\frac{2P_kR_k}{P_k+R_k},\\
  \mathrm{F1}_{\mathrm{macro}}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}F1_k .
  \end{gathered}
  \label{eq:prf}
\end{equation}
Macro averaging gives every class the same weight. On imbalanced data a model can reach a high accuracy while
ignoring the small classes, so we report accuracy together with macro precision, recall and F1, and use macro-F1
as the main metric.

% ================================================================================================ PART 2
\section{PART 2: PRACTICAL APPLICATION}

\subsection{I. Problem Description}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Title:} Time-of-day and weather classification of dashcam images on BDD100K using CNNs.
  \item \textbf{Objectives:} build a six-class task from the BDD100K tags; design and train a simple CNN, a CNN
        built from residual blocks and a ResNet50 transfer-learning model; compare them and analyse their errors.
        Knowing the lighting and the weather lets a driver-assistance system adapt its perception, which degrades
        at night, at dusk and in rain, fog or snow.
  \item \textbf{Input:} one RGB dashcam image ($1280\times720$, resized to $224\times224\times3$).
        \textbf{Output:} one of six classes (Table~\ref{tab:classes}), as a softmax probability vector.
  \item \textbf{Tasks performed:} label merging and cleaning, data split, resizing, normalization and
        augmentation; design and training of the three models (plus Model~1 without augmentation as an
        ablation); evaluation on the test set with accuracy, macro precision/recall/F1 and confusion matrices.
        Code: Keras~3 on the PyTorch backend \cite{chollet2015}, available at \cite{repo}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{table}[h]
\centering\small
\caption{The six target classes (class index in brackets).}
\label{tab:classes}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Time of day & Clear (clear, partly cloudy) & Unclear (overcast, rainy, snowy, foggy) \\
\midrule
Daytime   & daytime\_clear (0)  & daytime\_unclear (1)  \\
Night     & night\_clear (2)    & night\_unclear (3)    \\
Dawn/dusk & dawndusk\_clear (4) & dawndusk\_unclear (5) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsection{II. Dataset Description}
\textbf{BDD100K} \cite{yu2020} contains 100{,}000 dashcam images of $1280\times720$ pixels taken from driving
videos in the United States (download: Kaggle mirror \cite{kaggle},
\url{https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/solesensei/solesensei_bdd100k}). The images show ordinary road scenes -- cars,
buses, trucks, pedestrians, riders, bikes, traffic lights and signs -- and are annotated with object boxes and with
image-level tags for \emph{weather} (clear, partly cloudy, overcast, rainy, snowy, foggy), \emph{scene} and
\emph{time of day} (daytime, night, dawn/dusk). We use only the weather and time-of-day tags: images tagged
\emph{undefined} are removed, the time of day is kept, and the weather is merged into \textbf{clear} (clear, partly
cloudy) and \textbf{unclear} (overcast, rainy, snowy, foggy), which avoids tiny classes such as foggy images at
dusk. The official test labels are not public, so the official validation set is our \textbf{test set}, and the
official training set is split 80/20 (stratified, seed 42) into \textbf{training} and \textbf{validation} sets.
Table~\ref{tab:counts} gives the resulting 70{,}569 images.

The classes are strongly \textbf{imbalanced} -- night\_clear has 12 times more images than dawndusk\_unclear --
and some tags are visually ambiguous (Figure~\ref{fig:samples}): dawn/dusk ranges from almost-day to almost-night,
and partly cloudy (clear) skies can look like overcast (unclear) ones.

% ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ III
\subsection{III. CNN Model Design}

\subsubsection{1. Preprocessing and choices common to the three models}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Cleaning:} 8{,}135 training and 1{,}159 validation images with an \emph{undefined} tag were
        removed; every remaining image was decoded successfully, and the script checks that no image appears in two
        subsets.
  \item \textbf{Resizing and normalization:} images are resized once to $224\times224$ (the ResNet50 input size)
        and standardized with the ImageNet channel mean and standard deviation, so the three models share one
        input pipeline.
  \item \textbf{Augmentation:} only a random horizontal flip and a random zoom-in of up to 10\%. Brightness,
        contrast and colour changes are deliberately \emph{not} used: they are exactly the cues that separate day,
        dusk and night, or clear and hazy weather, so they would change the true class while keeping the old
        label. Vertical flips are excluded because the sky never appears at the bottom of a dashcam image.
  \item \textbf{Imbalance:} the loss (Eq.~\ref{eq:ce}) uses class weights $w_c = N/(K\,n_c)$, from 0.45 for
        night\_clear to 5.34 for dawndusk\_unclear, and the checkpoint kept for each model is the one with the best
        \textbf{validation macro-F1}, not accuracy.
  \item \textbf{Training:} Adam, learning rate halved after 2 epochs without improvement of the validation
        macro-F1, early stopping, mixed float16 precision, seed 42, one NVIDIA RTX 3060 (12~GB).
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{2. Model 1 -- Simple CNN}
\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{simple_cnn.png}
\caption{Architecture of Model 1. Numbers under the boxes are output shapes (height$^2\times$channels).}
\label{fig:simple}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Structure.} Four stages of a $3\times3$ convolution (ReLU) and a $2\times2$ max pooling with 32, 64, 128 and
128 filters reduce the image from $224\times224\times3$ to $14\times14\times128$; the result is flattened (25{,}088
values) and classified by a 256-unit dense layer, dropout 0.5 and a 6-way softmax (Figure~\ref{fig:simple},
Table~\ref{tab:simple}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering\small
\caption{Parameters of Model 1.}
\label{tab:simple}
\begin{tabular}{lrlr}
\toprule
Layer (output shape) & Parameters & Layer (output shape) & Parameters \\
\midrule
Conv $3\times3$, 32 ($224^2\times32$)  & 896     & Conv $3\times3$, 128 ($28^2\times128$) & 147{,}584 \\
Conv $3\times3$, 64 ($112^2\times64$)  & 18{,}496 & Flatten (25{,}088)                    & 0 \\
Conv $3\times3$, 128 ($56^2\times128$) & 73{,}856 & Dense 256 + Dropout 0.5               & 6{,}422{,}784 \\
$4\times$ MaxPool $2\times2$          & 0       & Dense 6, softmax                       & 1{,}542 \\
\midrule
                                      &         & \textbf{Total}                         & \textbf{6{,}665{,}158} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\textbf{Why this design.} Model~1 is the baseline required by the assignment and follows the classic LeNet/VGG
pattern conv $\rightarrow$ pool $\rightarrow\dots\rightarrow$ fully connected \cite{lecun1998,simonyan2015}. Four
pooling stages are needed to bring a $224\times224$ image to a small $14\times14$ grid; the number of filters doubles
while the resolution halves, which keeps the computation per stage similar, and is capped at 128 in the last stage
to keep the flattened vector and the first dense layer manageable. Even so, this dense layer holds 96\% of the
6.7~M parameters, which is why a strong dropout of 0.5 follows it. The model deliberately has no batch
normalization, no shortcuts and no blocks, so that the gain from these components can be measured with Model~2.
It is trained with batch size 64 and learning rate $10^{-3}$ for at most 20 epochs, once with augmentation
(\emph{Simple CNN + Aug}) and once without (\emph{Simple CNN}) to measure the effect of augmentation.

\subsubsection{3. Model 2 -- Complex CNN built from residual blocks}
\textbf{Structure.} The network is built from a reusable \textbf{ConvBlock} (Figure~\ref{fig:convblock}): a main
branch with two $3\times3$ convolutions, each followed by BN, with a ReLU between them; a shortcut branch with a
$1\times1$ convolution and BN that projects the input to the same number of channels; the two branches are added,
passed through a ReLU and a $2\times2$ max pooling. The full model (Figure~\ref{fig:complex},
Table~\ref{tab:complex}) is a stride-2 stem convolution (32 filters, BN, ReLU), four ConvBlocks with 64, 128, 256
and 512 channels, global average pooling and a head of dropout 0.3, a 256-unit dense layer, dropout 0.3 and the
softmax.

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\begin{minipage}[c]{0.36\textwidth}
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{conv_block.png}
  \caption{The ConvBlock of Model 2.}
  \label{fig:convblock}
\end{minipage}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[c]{0.6\textwidth}
  \centering\small
  \captionof{table}{Parameters of Model 2.}
  \label{tab:complex}
  \begin{tabular}{llr}
  \toprule
  Stage & Output & Parameters \\
  \midrule
  Stem conv /2 + BN       & $112^2\times32$ & 1{,}024 \\
  ConvBlock 1             & $56^2\times64$  & 58{,}304 \\
  ConvBlock 2             & $28^2\times128$ & 231{,}296 \\
  ConvBlock 3             & $14^2\times256$ & 921{,}344 \\
  ConvBlock 4             & $7^2\times512$  & 3{,}677{,}696 \\
  GAP                     & 512             & 0 \\
  Dense 256 + dropouts    & 256             & 131{,}328 \\
  Dense 6, softmax        & 6               & 1{,}542 \\
  \midrule
  \textbf{Total}          &                 & \textbf{5{,}022{,}534} \\
  \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{minipage}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{complex_cnn.png}
\caption{Architecture of Model 2. Numbers under the boxes are output shapes.}
\label{fig:complex}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Why this design.} Each choice addresses a weakness of Model~1:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \emph{Two $3\times3$ convolutions per block} (VGG) double the depth at each resolution and enlarge the
        receptive field cheaply, so the network can combine more local evidence (raindrops, wet road, snow patches)
        before pooling.
  \item \emph{Batch normalization} after every convolution stabilizes the training of the deeper network.
  \item \emph{Residual shortcuts} (ResNet) keep the deeper network easy to optimize; a $1\times1$ projection is
        needed because every block changes the number of channels.
  \item \emph{Global average pooling instead of flattening} removes the huge dense layer of Model~1 (the head now
        has only 133~K parameters) and matches the nature of the task: time of day and weather are \emph{global}
        properties of the scene -- overall brightness, sky colour, haze -- not the position of an object.
  \item \emph{A stride-2 stem} reduces the image to $112\times112$ immediately. Because the cues are global,
        full-resolution processing is unnecessary, and this cuts the computation and memory of the first block
        about four times.
\end{itemize}
The result is deeper (9 convolutions on the main path plus 4 shortcut convolutions) yet has fewer parameters than
Model~1 (5.0~M vs 6.7~M). It is trained with batch size 32, learning rate $3\times10^{-4}$ and weight decay
$10^{-4}$ for at most 25 epochs. The stem stride and the learning rate were chosen after two earlier runs
(Table~\ref{tab:iter}): with a stride-1 stem and learning rate $10^{-3}$ the validation F1 oscillated strongly, and
training either stopped early or took more than five hours.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering\small
\caption{Training runs of Model 2 (same blocks and number of parameters).}
\label{tab:iter}
\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
\toprule
Version & Stem stride & Learning rate & Batch & Epochs & Test macro-F1 & Time (min) \\
\midrule
v1 & 1 & $10^{-3}$ & 24 & 20 & 0.6888 & 310 \\
v2 & 1 & $10^{-3}$ & 32 & 10 (early stop) & 0.6384 & 153 \\
\textbf{final} & \textbf{2} & $\mathbf{3\times10^{-4}}$ & \textbf{32} & \textbf{21} & \textbf{0.6927} & \textbf{94} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsubsection{4. Model 3 -- Transfer learning with ResNet50}
\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.95\textwidth]{resnet50_transfer.png}
\caption{Architecture of Model 3 (grey: pretrained backbone; green: new head).}
\label{fig:resnet}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Structure.} The ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 \cite{he2016} backbone without its top ($7\times7$ stem, max
pooling and 16 bottleneck blocks in four stages, 23.6~M parameters) turns the image into a $7\times7\times2048$
tensor; a new head of GAP, dropout 0.3 and a 6-way softmax (12{,}294 parameters) is added
(Figure~\ref{fig:resnet}). A small ``to Caffe'' layer converts our ImageNet-standardized input into the BGR,
mean-subtracted format the Keras weights were trained with. Training has two stages: (1) backbone frozen, only the
head trained for at most 3 epochs at learning rate $10^{-3}$; (2) all layers unfrozen and fine-tuned for at most 10
epochs at $10^{-4}$ with weight decay $10^{-4}$ and batch size 32.

\textbf{Why this design.} ResNet50 is the standard backbone for transfer learning: its ImageNet features (edges,
colours, textures, illumination) are useful for road scenes; it belongs to the same residual family as Model~2,
which makes the comparison ``own design vs.\ pretrained design'' fair; and with 23.6~M parameters it can be
fine-tuned with batch 32 on a 12~GB GPU. The head is kept minimal (GAP and one linear layer) so that the result
reflects the pretrained features rather than a large new classifier. The two-stage schedule protects the pretrained
weights from the large gradients of a randomly initialized head, and the ten times smaller learning rate in stage~2
adapts the features instead of overwriting them \cite{yosinski2014}.

% ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ IV
\subsection{IV. Experimental Results}

\subsubsection{1. Results on the test set}
Table~\ref{tab:main} gives the results of the four trained models on the 8{,}841 test images (precision, recall and
F1-score are macro-averaged; the best value of each column is in bold).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering\small
\caption{Results on the test set. ``Epochs'' gives the epochs run and the epoch with the best validation macro-F1.}
\label{tab:main}
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4.5pt}
\begin{tabular}{lccccccc}
\toprule
Model & Accuracy & Precision & Recall & F1-score & Params & Epochs & Time (min) \\
\midrule
Simple CNN                & 0.7559 & 0.5918 & 0.5953 & 0.5928 & 6.67 M & 18 / 13 & 17 \\
Simple CNN + Aug          & 0.7768 & 0.6213 & 0.6517 & 0.6333 & 6.67 M & 19 / 14 & 31 \\
Complex CNN + Aug         & 0.8098 & 0.6769 & \best{0.7177} & \best{0.6927} & 5.02 M & 21 / 16 & 94 \\
ResNet50 + Aug + Transfer & \best{0.8112} & \best{0.6924} & 0.6805 & 0.6817 & 23.60 M & 3+8 / 3+5 & 81 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The two strongest models are close: the \textbf{complex CNN} has the best macro-F1 (0.6927) and recall,
\textbf{ResNet50} the best accuracy (0.8112) and precision. All models are far above the trivial ``always
night\_clear'' baseline (37.1\% accuracy, macro-F1 below 0.10). Accuracy is 12--16 points higher than macro-F1 for
every model, the signature of class imbalance: the large classes are recognized well, the small ones pull the macro
average down. For every model the best validation macro-F1 is within one point of the test macro-F1, so
checkpoint selection did not over-fit the validation set.

\subsubsection{2. Learning curves}
\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{learning_curves.png}
\caption{Validation macro-F1, validation loss and over-fitting gap (training minus validation accuracy) per epoch,
from the training logs. For ResNet50, epochs 1--3 are stage 1 and epochs 4--11 stage 2.}
\label{fig:curves}
\end{figure}

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Without augmentation} the simple CNN over-fits quickly (Figure~\ref{fig:curves}): its training
        accuracy reaches 0.93 while the validation accuracy stays near 0.75, and the validation loss rises from 0.87
        to 2.26. \textbf{With augmentation} the gap stays much smaller and the validation loss only rises to 1.13.
  \item The \textbf{complex CNN} shows almost no over-fitting once training has settled (gap close to zero), thanks
        to BN, GAP and weight decay. Its validation F1 fluctuates during the first ten epochs (down to 0.35) because
        the BN running statistics lag behind the quickly changing weights; the curve stabilizes once the learning
        rate is reduced.
  \item \textbf{ResNet50} learns fastest: after one epoch with a frozen backbone it already reaches 0.78 validation
        accuracy. Fine-tuning brings the best validation F1 (0.687) within five epochs, after which the large network
        over-fits (training accuracy 0.90) and early stopping restores the best checkpoint.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{3. Per-class results}
\begin{table}[h]
\centering\small
\caption{F1-score per class, and accuracy on the two sub-tasks derived from the six-class predictions.}
\label{tab:perclass}

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.64\textwidth]{confusion_matrices.png}
\caption{Row-normalized confusion matrices on the test set (D = daytime, N = night, DD = dawn/dusk; C = clear,
U = unclear).}
\label{fig:cm}
\end{figure}

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Class ranking} (Table~\ref{tab:perclass}). night\_clear is the easiest class for every model; the rare
        night\_unclear and dawn/dusk classes are the hardest, dawndusk\_unclear staying below 0.41. Every
        improvement helps the small classes most: from Simple CNN to Complex CNN the F1 of night\_unclear rises from
        0.40 to 0.64, that of night\_clear only from 0.87 to 0.91.
  \item \textbf{Time of day} is the easier sub-task (92--93\%), night being almost perfect. The errors come from
        dawn/dusk: 27--39\% of the dawn/dusk images are predicted as daytime (Figure~\ref{fig:cm}), because
        dawn/dusk is a continuum and its boundary with day is subjective.
  \item \textbf{Weather} is harder (81--86\%). Partly cloudy skies, merged into \emph{clear}, are often taken for
        overcast (only 75.5\% correct for the complex CNN and 60.4\% for ResNet50); this is why ResNet50 labels 22\%
        of the daytime\_clear images as daytime\_unclear. At night the sky is invisible -- BDD100K has only 144
        overcast or partly cloudy night images out of 31{,}392 -- so \emph{unclear} means rain or snow, and wet roads
        or reflections cause most night\_clear $\leftrightarrow$ night\_unclear errors. Snowy images improve the most
        with model capacity (from 57.6\% correct for Simple CNN + Aug to 86.1\% for ResNet50).
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{4. Discussion}
\textbf{Augmentation} (Simple CNN $\rightarrow$ Simple CNN + Aug) improves accuracy by 2.1 points and macro-F1 by
4.1 points with the same network: the mild, label-preserving transformations regularize the large dense layer
without adding label noise. \textbf{CNN blocks} (Simple CNN + Aug $\rightarrow$ Complex CNN) add 3.3 points of
accuracy and 5.9 points of macro-F1 with 25\% fewer parameters, which confirms the design choices of Section III.3:
BN and shortcuts make a deeper network trainable, and GAP spends the parameters on feature extraction instead of
memorization. \textbf{Transfer learning} gives the fastest convergence, the highest accuracy and precision and the
best night classes, but not a better macro-F1 than the complex CNN (0.6817 vs 0.6927). ImageNet features are
object-centric while our classes depend on global illumination and haze, the 23.6~M-parameter network over-fits
after a few fine-tuning epochs, and its schedule was not tuned. With a single run per model, a one-point difference
is within seed-to-seed variation, so the two models are best seen as comparable with complementary strengths. The
complex CNN is also cheaper, with 4.7 times fewer parameters than ResNet50.

% ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ V
\subsection{V. Conclusion}
We classified 70{,}569 BDD100K dashcam images into six time-of-day $\times$ weather classes with three CNNs. The
\textbf{complex CNN} built from residual ConvBlocks with BN, a stride-2 stem and global average pooling achieved the
best macro-F1 (\textbf{0.6927}, accuracy 0.8098) with only 5.0~M parameters; \textbf{ResNet50} with two-stage
fine-tuning achieved the best accuracy (\textbf{0.8112}, macro-F1 0.6817); the simple CNN reached a macro-F1 of
0.6333 with augmentation and 0.5928 without. Label-preserving augmentation and residual blocks each brought a clear
gain, and design choices matched to the global nature of the task (early down-sampling, GAP) made the model both
more accurate and cheaper. The remaining errors concentrate on dawn/dusk images, partly cloudy skies and rain at
night, where the labels themselves are ambiguous. \textbf{Limitations:} one training run per model, square
$224\times224$ inputs and no systematic hyper-parameter search. \textbf{Future work:} separate output heads for time
of day and weather, higher-resolution inputs, losses designed for imbalanced data and an ensemble of the complex CNN
and ResNet50.
